abdomen.clinical: The abdomen houses the gut, liver, spleen, pancreas and kidneys; localizing pain to a quadrant guides the differential for appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis and renal colic.
abdomen.imaging: Axial CT from diaphragm to iliac crest shows solid organs, bowel loops and retroperitoneal fat planes in one pass, the standard survey for acute abdominal pain.

adrenal-gland.clinical: Adrenal incidentalomas are common on cross sectional imaging; size, growth and washout characteristics separate benign adenomas from pheochromocytoma or metastasis.
adrenal-gland.imaging: Seen as a Y or V shaped structure capping each kidney on axial CT or MRI; unenhanced density and contrast washout help characterize a nodule.

amygdala.clinical: Amygdala volume and signal changes are studied in temporal lobe epilepsy and mesial temporal sclerosis, often alongside the adjacent hippocampus.
amygdala.imaging: An almond shaped grey matter mass at the anteromedial temporal lobe, best seen on coronal T1 or T2 MRI just anterior to the hippocampal head.

aorta.clinical: The abdominal aorta is the classic site for atherosclerotic aneurysm, which can rupture; wall calcification, dissection flaps and branch vessel involvement are key findings.
aorta.imaging: Traced as a midline retroperitoneal tubular structure anterior to the vertebral bodies on axial CT; diameter over three centimetres suggests aneurysm.

autochthonous-back-muscle.clinical: These paraspinal muscles stabilize and extend the spine; their atrophy or fatty infiltration is linked to chronic low back pain and degenerative disc disease.
autochthonous-back-muscle.imaging: Seen as paired muscle bundles flanking the spinous processes on axial CT or MRI of the spine, deep to the more superficial back musculature.

brachiocephalic-trunk.clinical: The first branch of the aortic arch; it can be involved in arch dissection or atherosclerosis, and a high-riding trunk crossing in front of the trachea matters in tracheostomy.
brachiocephalic-trunk.imaging: On axial CT it lies anterior and to the right of the trachea above the arch, between the right brachiocephalic vein and the left common carotid artery.

brachiocephalic-vein.clinical: A common site for central venous catheters; thrombosis or stenosis here from lines or pacing leads causes arm and facial swelling, and tumour can invade it in the superior mediastinum.
brachiocephalic-vein.imaging: The left vein crosses in front of the arch branches just behind the manubrium, longer and more horizontal than the right; arm-side contrast injection can leave dense streak artefact in it.

brain.clinical: Brain imaging screens for stroke, haemorrhage, tumour and trauma; grey white differentiation and midline position are checked on every scan before finer review.
brain.imaging: CT shows brain parenchyma as grey and white matter density within the calvarium; MRI gives superior soft tissue contrast on T1 and T2 sequences.

brainstem.clinical: The brainstem carries the long motor and sensory tracts and most cranial nerve nuclei; even small lesions here can cause disproportionate deficits or coma.
brainstem.imaging: Identified as the column linking the cerebrum to the spinal cord, anterior to the cerebellum and fourth ventricle on sagittal and axial MRI.

caudate-nucleus.clinical: The caudate is part of the basal ganglia circuit involved in movement disorders such as Huntington disease, which causes characteristic caudate atrophy.
caudate-nucleus.imaging: Its head bulges into the lateral ventricle's frontal horn, seen as a comma shaped grey matter structure on axial CT or MRI at the level of the basal ganglia.

cerebellar-cortex.clinical: Cerebellar cortical atrophy or infarction produces ataxia, dysmetria and gait imbalance; it is a common site for metastasis and stroke in the posterior fossa.
cerebellar-cortex.imaging: The thin folded grey matter rim over the cerebellar folia, best assessed on axial or coronal MRI of the posterior fossa.

cerebellar-white-matter.clinical: Cerebellar white matter lesions occur in demyelinating disease and can also be the site of haemorrhagic infarction within the posterior fossa.
cerebellar-white-matter.imaging: The central white core of the cerebellum deep to the folia, seen as a branching arbor vitae pattern on sagittal MRI.

cerebellum.clinical: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance; posterior fossa strokes or tumours here can cause acute obstructive hydrocephalus and are a neurosurgical emergency.
cerebellum.imaging: Occupies the posterior cranial fossa below the tentorium, best seen on axial and sagittal CT or MRI alongside the brainstem and fourth ventricle.

cerebral-cortex.clinical: Cortical grey matter loss, oedema or contrast enhancement points to atrophy, infarction, encephalitis or tumour depending on distribution and pattern.
cerebral-cortex.imaging: The outer grey matter mantle of the cerebrum, traced along the gyri and sulci on axial or coronal CT and MRI.

cerebral-white-matter.clinical: Cerebral white matter is the site of small vessel ischaemic disease, demyelination and diffuse axonal injury after trauma.
cerebral-white-matter.imaging: Appears as the hypodense or T2 hyperintense region deep to the cortex on CT and MRI, containing the projection, association and commissural fibres.

cervical-vertebra.clinical: Cervical vertebral fractures and cord compression from trauma or degenerative disease are urgent concerns; alignment and canal diameter are checked on every trauma scan.
cervical-vertebra.imaging: The seven cervical vertebrae are counted from the skull base to the thoracic junction on sagittal CT or MRI, each bearing a transverse foramen for the vertebral artery.

clavicle.clinical: The clavicle is a frequently fractured bone, especially in falls onto the shoulder, and its position guides assessment of thoracic outlet structures.
clavicle.imaging: A slender S shaped bone crossing the upper thorax, seen in cross section on axial CT and along its length on coronal reformats or plain radiograph.

colon.clinical: Colonic pathology includes diverticulitis, colitis and colorectal cancer; wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding and haustral pattern are the key CT signs.
colon.imaging: Identified by its haustra and peripheral course framing the abdomen on axial CT, distinguishing it from small bowel loops.

common-carotid-artery.clinical: Atherosclerotic disease is usually at the carotid bifurcation, a major cause of stroke; the common carotid pulse is the one felt in the neck, and the vessel is at risk in penetrating neck trauma.
common-carotid-artery.imaging: Round enhancing vessel in the carotid sheath beside the trachea and thyroid, medial to the internal jugular vein; CT angiography shows stenosis, dissection and calcified plaque.

corona-radiata.clinical: Lesions in the corona radiata, such as lacunar infarcts, can interrupt motor or sensory fibres and produce a pure hemiparesis or hemisensory syndrome.
corona-radiata.imaging: A fan shaped band of white matter above the internal capsule, seen radiating toward the cortex on axial MRI.

corpus-callosum.clinical: The corpus callosum can be involved by demyelination, diffuse axonal injury or agenesis; its shape and signal are assessed whenever midline pathology is suspected.
corpus-callosum.imaging: The thick white matter band arching over the lateral ventricles, best seen on midline sagittal MRI.

duodenum.clinical: The duodenum is a common site for peptic ulcer disease and is closely related to the pancreatic head, so pathology here can affect both structures.
duodenum.imaging: Its C shaped course wraps around the pancreatic head, traced on axial CT of the upper abdomen just distal to the pylorus.

esophagus.clinical: The oesophagus is assessed for strictures, varices and malignancy; wall thickening on cross sectional imaging raises concern for tumour or oesophagitis.
esophagus.imaging: A midline muscular tube seen posterior to the trachea on axial CT of the neck and chest, best evaluated with oral contrast or endoscopy.

femur.clinical: The femur is the most common site of osteoporotic hip fracture and a frequent location for primary bone tumours in younger patients.
femur.imaging: The longest bone in the body, seen in the thigh on coronal and axial CT or MRI with a well corticated shaft and rounded femoral head proximally.

fibula.clinical: The fibula bears little weight but its fracture, often paired with a tibial or ankle injury, affects ankle joint stability.
fibula.imaging: The slender lateral bone of the leg, seen alongside the larger tibia on axial CT or MRI of the lower leg.

foot.clinical: Foot imaging evaluates fractures, especially of the calcaneus and metatarsals after a fall, and degenerative or diabetic changes affecting weight bearing.
foot.imaging: The tarsal, metatarsal and phalangeal bones are surveyed together on sagittal, coronal and axial CT of the foot.

fornix.clinical: The fornix carries hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies and thalamus; its injury contributes to memory impairment in some amnestic syndromes.
fornix.imaging: A thin arched white matter band beneath the corpus callosum, traced on sagittal and coronal MRI toward the mammillary bodies.

fourth-ventricle.clinical: Obstruction of the fourth ventricle by a posterior fossa mass causes acute hydrocephalus and is a neurosurgical emergency in children and adults.
fourth-ventricle.imaging: A midline cerebrospinal fluid space between the pons and cerebellum, seen as a triangular fluid signal on axial and sagittal MRI.

frontal-lobe.clinical: Frontal lobe injury or tumour can alter personality, judgement and motor function, and this lobe is a common site of contusion after head trauma.
frontal-lobe.imaging: Lies anterior to the central sulcus, occupying the front of the cerebral hemisphere on axial and sagittal CT or MRI.

gallbladder.clinical: The gallbladder is the site of gallstones and cholecystitis; wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid and stones are the classic imaging triad.
gallbladder.imaging: A pear shaped fluid filled sac beneath the liver, seen on axial CT or ultrasound of the right upper quadrant.

globus-pallidus.clinical: The globus pallidus is affected in carbon monoxide poisoning, kernicterus and some metabolic disorders, often with characteristic bilateral signal change.
globus-pallidus.imaging: The medial, paler part of the lentiform nucleus, seen medial to the putamen on axial MRI of the basal ganglia.

gluteal-muscle.clinical: Gluteal muscle atrophy or tear affects hip abduction and gait, and this region is a common site for intramuscular injection related complications.
gluteal-muscle.imaging: The buttock musculature seen on axial CT or MRI of the pelvis, overlying the posterior ilium and hip joint.

hand.clinical: Hand imaging evaluates trauma, arthritis and soft tissue infection; joint space narrowing and erosions here are early clues to rheumatoid arthritis.
hand.imaging: The carpal, metacarpal and phalangeal bones and joints are surveyed together on radiograph or CT of the hand.

hand-bone.clinical: Carpal and metacarpal fractures, especially of the scaphoid, and erosive arthritis are common reasons to image the hand skeleton.
hand-bone.imaging: The eight carpal bones, five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges are identified together on hand radiograph or CT, the scaphoid being the key carpal to scrutinize.

head.clinical: Head imaging is the frontline study after trauma or in acute neurological deficit, screening the skull, brain and extracranial soft tissues together.
head.imaging: Encompasses the skull vault, base and brain on a single CT or MRI series, read from the scalp inward for fracture, haemorrhage and mass effect.

heart.clinical: Cardiac chamber size, wall thickness and coronary calcium are assessed on CT and MRI to evaluate heart failure, ischaemic disease and valvular pathology.
heart.imaging: A muscular organ occupying the middle mediastinum, seen on axial CT of the thorax with its chambers best distinguished on gated CT or cardiac MRI.

hip-bone.clinical: Hip bone fractures occur with pelvic trauma and osteoporotic falls; acetabular fracture pattern determines surgical planning.
hip-bone.imaging: Formed by the fused ilium, ischium and pubis, seen as the bony pelvic ring on axial and coronal CT of the pelvis.

hippocampus.clinical: Hippocampal atrophy or T2 signal change is a hallmark of mesial temporal sclerosis and is also assessed in early Alzheimer disease.
hippocampus.imaging: A curved grey matter structure in the medial temporal lobe floor, best evaluated on coronal MRI angled along the temporal lobe axis.

iliac-artery.clinical: Iliac artery aneurysm, occlusive disease and dissection are assessed on CT angiography, particularly before pelvic or vascular intervention.
iliac-artery.imaging: The paired vessels arising from the aortic bifurcation, traced along the pelvic sidewalls on axial CT with contrast.

iliac-vein.clinical: Iliac vein compression or thrombosis, including May-Thurner syndrome, is a cause of unilateral leg swelling and deep vein thrombosis.
iliac-vein.imaging: Seen running alongside the iliac artery on axial CT or MRI of the pelvis, draining into the inferior vena cava.

iliopsoas.clinical: The iliopsoas can harbour an abscess or haematoma, presenting with hip flexion pain, and is assessed in cases of retroperitoneal bleeding on anticoagulation.
iliopsoas.imaging: A muscle bundle running along the posterior abdominal wall and pelvic brim to the lesser trochanter, seen on axial CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis.

inferior-vena-cava.clinical: The inferior vena cava is evaluated for thrombus, tumour invasion by renal or hepatic malignancy, and filter placement in venous thromboembolic disease.
inferior-vena-cava.imaging: A midline to right sided venous structure anterior to the spine on axial CT, best distinguished from the aorta by its ovoid, thin walled shape.

insula.clinical: The insula is involved in seizure semiology and stroke localization, and its cortex sits at a common site for middle cerebral artery territory infarcts.
insula.imaging: Buried within the lateral fissure, seen on axial and coronal MRI deep to the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula.

internal-capsule.clinical: A small lacunar infarct in the internal capsule can cause a dense pure motor hemiparesis because descending motor fibres are tightly packed here.
internal-capsule.imaging: A white matter band between the caudate and lentiform nucleus, seen as a V shaped structure on axial MRI at the level of the basal ganglia.

kidney.clinical: The kidneys are evaluated for stones, masses, hydronephrosis and infection; cortical thinning and scarring reflect chronic disease.
kidney.imaging: Paired retroperitoneal organs seen on either side of the spine on axial CT, with the collecting system best assessed on delayed contrast phases.

lateral-ventricle.clinical: Lateral ventricular enlargement suggests hydrocephalus or atrophy, while asymmetry can indicate a mass lesion obstructing one foramen of Monro.
lateral-ventricle.imaging: Two C shaped cerebrospinal fluid spaces within the cerebral hemispheres, seen on axial and coronal CT or MRI flanking the septum pellucidum.

liver.clinical: The liver is assessed for cirrhosis, focal lesions and metastasis; contrast enhancement pattern across phases is central to characterizing a hepatic mass.
liver.imaging: The largest abdominal organ, filling the right upper quadrant on axial CT with a smooth capsule and homogeneous parenchyma in health.

lower-limb.clinical: Lower limb imaging surveys the femur, tibia, fibula and foot together after trauma or for vascular and soft tissue disease affecting the whole limb.
lower-limb.imaging: The thigh, leg and foot are imaged in continuity on coronal CT or MRI reformats to assess alignment and length.

lower-lobe-left.clinical: The left lower lobe is a common site for aspiration pneumonia and is assessed for consolidation, nodules and effusion on chest imaging.
lower-lobe-left.imaging: Lies posteroinferior to the oblique fissure on axial CT of the thorax, best distinguished from the lingula on sagittal reformats.

lower-lobe-right.clinical: The right lower lobe is frequently involved by aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary embolism related infarct and lower lobe predominant fibrosis.
lower-lobe-right.imaging: Located below and behind the oblique fissure on axial CT, the largest lobe of the right lung on cross section.

lumbar-vertebra.clinical: Lumbar vertebrae are the most common site of disc herniation and degenerative disease causing low back pain and radiculopathy.
lumbar-vertebra.imaging: The five largest movable vertebrae, counted on sagittal CT or MRI of the lumbar spine between the thoracic and sacral segments.

lung.clinical: The lungs are assessed for nodules, consolidation, embolism and fibrosis; lobar anatomy determines how findings are localized and described.
lung.imaging: Air filled parenchyma seen as low density on CT windowed for lung detail, with fissures separating the lobes on axial and coronal images.

metatarsal.clinical: Metatarsal stress fractures are common in runners and the fifth metatarsal base fracture is a classic ankle inversion injury.
metatarsal.imaging: Five long bones between the tarsus and toes, seen in sequence on dorsoplantar radiograph or axial CT of the foot.

middle-lobe-right.clinical: The right middle lobe is prone to chronic atelectasis and bronchiectasis, sometimes called middle lobe syndrome, from bronchial compression.
middle-lobe-right.imaging: A wedge shaped lobe between the horizontal and oblique fissures, best delineated on coronal or sagittal CT reformats of the right lung.

neck.clinical: The neck packs the airway, oesophagus, thyroid, great vessels and cervical spine into a small space, so infection, tumour or haematoma can threaten the airway and spread along fascial planes into the mediastinum.
neck.imaging: Contrast-enhanced CT from skull base to aortic arch is the standard survey; the fat planes around the carotid sheath, visceral space and prevertebral space show where a mass or collection lies.

nucleus-accumbens.clinical: The nucleus accumbens is part of the reward circuitry studied in addiction and is a deep brain stimulation target in some psychiatric disorders.
nucleus-accumbens.imaging: A small grey mass where the caudate head and putamen merge anteriorly, seen on coronal MRI at the level of the anterior commissure.

occipital-lobe.clinical: The occipital lobe contains the primary visual cortex; infarction here classically produces a homonymous visual field defect.
occipital-lobe.imaging: Forms the posterior pole of the cerebral hemisphere, seen on axial and sagittal CT or MRI behind the parieto-occipital sulcus.

pancreas.clinical: The pancreas is central to acute and chronic pancreatitis and harbours both cystic and solid tumours with distinct imaging appearances.
pancreas.imaging: A transverse gland behind the stomach on axial CT, running from the duodenal C loop to the splenic hilum.

paranasal-sinus.clinical: The paranasal sinuses are commonly affected by sinusitis, polyps and, rarely, sinonasal tumours that can erode adjacent bone.
paranasal-sinus.imaging: Air filled cavities within the frontal, maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid bones, seen as low density spaces on coronal CT of the face.

parietal-lobe.clinical: Parietal lobe lesions cause sensory neglect, apraxia or sensory deficits depending on the hemisphere involved, and this lobe is a common stroke territory.
parietal-lobe.imaging: Lies behind the central sulcus and above the parieto-occipital sulcus, seen on axial and sagittal CT or MRI.

pelvis.clinical: Pelvic imaging evaluates fracture after trauma, and in nontrauma settings surveys the bladder, prostate or gynaecological organs and bowel together.
pelvis.imaging: The bony pelvic ring and its contained viscera are seen together on axial CT from the iliac crest to the pubic symphysis.

phalanx-foot.clinical: Toe phalanx fractures, often from a stubbing injury, and hallux valgus deformity are common reasons to image these bones.
phalanx-foot.imaging: Fourteen small bones forming the toes, three per lesser toe and two in the great toe, seen on radiograph or axial CT of the forefoot.

portal-vein.clinical: Portal vein thrombosis and tumour thrombus are important findings in cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, altering management.
portal-vein.imaging: Formed by the confluence of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, traced into the liver hilum on axial or coronal CT with contrast.

prostate.clinical: The prostate is screened for benign hyperplasia and cancer; zonal anatomy on MRI guides lesion localization for biopsy.
prostate.imaging: Sits below the bladder in the male pelvis, best characterized by zonal anatomy on multiparametric MRI or as a homogeneous mass on axial CT.

putamen.clinical: The putamen is a common site for hypertensive haemorrhage and shows characteristic signal change in some neurodegenerative disorders.
putamen.imaging: The outer, larger part of the lentiform nucleus, seen lateral to the globus pallidus on axial MRI of the basal ganglia.

rib.clinical: Rib fractures are assessed for flail chest and underlying lung or splenic injury after trauma, and lytic rib lesions raise concern for metastasis.
rib.imaging: Elastic arched bones forming the thoracic cage, best traced along their curved course on coronal or 3D reformatted CT of the chest.

sacrum.clinical: Sacral fractures, often insufficiency fractures in osteoporotic bone, and sacroiliitis are key indications for sacral imaging.
sacrum.imaging: A triangular bone formed by fused sacral vertebrae, seen at the posterior pelvic ring on axial and sagittal CT.

skull.clinical: Skull fractures, especially depressed or basilar patterns, and calvarial lesions are assessed on head CT after trauma.
skull.imaging: The bony covering of the head, seen as a dense rim on axial CT in bone window, comprising the cranial vault and base.

small-bowel.clinical: Small bowel obstruction, Crohn disease and ischaemia are the leading indications for small bowel imaging, with wall thickening and dilation as key signs.
small-bowel.imaging: The jejunum and ileum are traced as a mesenteric mass of loops on axial CT, distinguished from colon by their smaller calibre and valvulae.

spinal-cord.clinical: Spinal cord compression from disc herniation, tumour or trauma is a surgical emergency when it threatens permanent neurological deficit.
spinal-cord.imaging: A continuous cord of neural tissue within the vertebral canal, seen centrally on sagittal MRI, the modality of choice over CT.

spleen.clinical: The spleen is vulnerable to traumatic laceration and rupture and is enlarged in portal hypertension, infection and haematological disease.
spleen.imaging: A vascular organ in the left upper quadrant on axial CT, similar in density to the liver and adjacent to the left kidney and stomach.

sternum.clinical: Sternal fracture suggests a high energy chest injury and raises concern for underlying cardiac or great vessel trauma.
sternum.imaging: A flat midline bone at the front of the chest, seen on axial CT anterior to the heart and best profiled on sagittal reformats.

stomach.clinical: The stomach is evaluated for gastritis, ulcer and malignancy; wall thickening on CT can be the first clue to gastric cancer.
stomach.imaging: A dilated J shaped segment of the digestive tract in the left upper abdomen, distended by oral contrast or air on axial CT.

subarachnoid-space.clinical: Blood in the subarachnoid space signals aneurysmal or traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage, a neurological emergency needing urgent vascular workup.
subarachnoid-space.imaging: A thin cerebrospinal fluid filled space between the arachnoid and pia mater, seen along the cortical sulci on CT and MRI.

subclavian-artery.clinical: Subclavian stenosis can cause arm claudication or steal from the vertebral artery; the artery is also compressed in thoracic outlet syndrome and is a landmark for central line placement.
subclavian-artery.imaging: Arches over the lung apex behind the clavicle and between the scalene muscles; best followed on coronal or oblique reformats of a CT angiogram.

superior-vena-cava.clinical: Obstruction, most often from lung cancer, lymphoma or thrombosed catheters, causes superior vena cava syndrome with facial and arm swelling; it is the target position for central line tips.
superior-vena-cava.imaging: Oval vessel to the right of the ascending aorta on axial CT, draining into the right atrium; collateral veins on the chest wall suggest obstruction.

tarsal.clinical: Tarsal fractures, particularly of the calcaneus and talus, follow axial loading injuries such as a fall from height.
tarsal.imaging: Seven bones including the calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuboid and cuneiforms, seen at the hindfoot and midfoot on CT or radiograph.

telencephalon.clinical: The telencephalon comprises the cerebral hemispheres and basal ganglia, the level at which most cortical and subcortical pathology is localized.
telencephalon.imaging: The cerebral hemispheres and their deep grey nuclei, seen together on axial MRI above the diencephalon.

temporal-lobe.clinical: The temporal lobe, including the hippocampus, is the classic site of origin for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy and is a common contusion site after trauma.
temporal-lobe.imaging: Lies below the lateral fissure, seen on axial and coronal CT or MRI extending back toward the occipital lobe.

thalamus.clinical: Thalamic haemorrhage is a common hypertensive bleed location and thalamic infarcts can cause disproportionate sensory or consciousness disturbance.
thalamus.imaging: A large ovoid grey matter mass flanking the third ventricle, seen on axial MRI at the level of the basal ganglia.

third-ventricle.clinical: Obstruction of the third ventricle, for example by a colloid cyst, causes intermittent headache from acute hydrocephalus.
third-ventricle.imaging: A narrow midline cerebrospinal fluid cleft between the two thalami, best seen on coronal and sagittal MRI.

thoracic-cage.clinical: The thoracic cage protects the heart and lungs; fracture patterns here indicate the force of chest trauma and risk of underlying organ injury.
thoracic-cage.imaging: Formed by the ribs, sternum and thoracic vertebrae, seen as the bony chest wall on axial and 3D reformatted CT.

thoracic-vertebra.clinical: Thoracic vertebral compression fractures are common in osteoporosis and are assessed for height loss and canal encroachment.
thoracic-vertebra.imaging: Twelve vertebrae distinguished by their costal facets for rib articulation, counted on sagittal CT or MRI of the spine.

thorax.clinical: Thoracic imaging screens the heart, lungs, mediastinum and chest wall together, the primary study for chest pain, dyspnoea and trauma.
thorax.imaging: The chest cavity from thoracic inlet to diaphragm, surveyed on axial CT with lung and mediastinal windows read separately.

thyroid-gland.clinical: Thyroid nodules are common incidental findings on neck and chest CT; a large goitre can compress the trachea or extend behind the sternum, and nodules are characterised by ultrasound rather than CT.
thyroid-gland.imaging: Two lobes and an isthmus draped around the front of the trachea; it is brighter than muscle on unenhanced CT because of its iodine content and enhances strongly after contrast.

tibia.clinical: The tibia bears most lower leg weight and is a common site for stress fracture, open fracture after trauma and osteomyelitis.
tibia.imaging: The medial, larger bone of the leg, seen on axial and coronal CT or MRI with the fibula lying laterally.

trachea.clinical: The trachea can be narrowed by intubation injury, extrinsic compression from goitre or tumour, or airway malacia; its position also flags mediastinal shift from tension pneumothorax or collapse.
trachea.imaging: An air-filled tube anterior to the oesophagus from about C6 to the carina, round or horseshoe shaped on axial CT and best assessed on lung window; coronal images show its course and any deviation.

upper-lobe-left.clinical: The left upper lobe, including the lingula, is assessed for apical scarring, nodules and the site of many primary lung cancers.
upper-lobe-left.imaging: Occupies the anterosuperior left hemithorax on axial CT, separated from the lower lobe by the oblique fissure.

upper-lobe-right.clinical: The right upper lobe is a classic site for reactivation tuberculosis, aspiration in some positions, and primary lung cancer; lobar collapse gives a characteristic shape on the chest radiograph.
upper-lobe-right.imaging: Occupies the anterosuperior right hemithorax on axial CT, bounded below by the horizontal fissure and behind by the oblique fissure; the fissures are best seen on thin lung-window images.

urinary-bladder.clinical: The bladder is evaluated for stones, tumour and trauma related rupture; wall thickening can reflect chronic outlet obstruction or cystitis.
urinary-bladder.imaging: A musculomembranous reservoir in the anterior pelvis, seen as a fluid filled structure on axial CT, best distended for optimal wall assessment.

ventral-diencephalon.clinical: This composite region groups the hypothalamus, subthalamic nucleus and related structures, relevant to endocrine, movement and consciousness disorders.
ventral-diencephalon.imaging: A deep midline region below the thalamus, identified on coronal MRI near the mammillary bodies and cerebral peduncles; not a single named structure.

vertebral-canal.clinical: The vertebral canal contains the spinal cord and nerve roots; its narrowing, or stenosis, causes claudication or radiculopathy.
vertebral-canal.imaging: The continuous bony tunnel formed by successive vertebral foramina, traced on sagittal CT or MRI alongside the spinal cord.

vertebral-column.clinical: The vertebral column provides axial support and protects the spinal cord; its alignment and curvature are assessed in trauma and degenerative disease.
vertebral-column.imaging: The chain of cervical, thoracic, lumbar and sacral segments, seen in continuity on sagittal CT or MRI reformats.
